copyright: Green-crowned brilliant hummingbirds feeding on lobster-claw flowers, Costa Rica (© Paul Hobson/Nature Picture Library)
description: When it comes to aerial acrobatics, hummingbirds are in a league of their own. Found only in the Americas, these tiny birds can hover in place, fly backwards and beat their wings dozens of times per second. As they visit flowers in search of nectar, they also serve as important pollinators, helping sustain ecosystems from alpine meadows to tropical rainforests. Their shimmering plumage, remarkable agility and high-energy lifestyles make them some of the world's most fascinating birds.

copyright: Westerheversand Lighthouse in Westerhever, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany (© bluejayphoto/Getty Images)
description: Rising above the salt marshes along Germany's North Sea coast, the Westerheversand Lighthouse is instantly recognisable thanks to its distinctive red-and-white stripes. Built between 1906 and 1908, the lighthouse has stood as an icon on the Eiderstedt Peninsula for more than a century, guiding ships through the waters of the North Sea. Today, it remains one of northern Germany's best-known coastal landmarks. Visitors who climb its 157 steps are rewarded with sweeping views of the surrounding scenery.

copyright: Coyote Buttes, Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, Arizona, United States (© James Hager/Getty Images)
description: Blink and you'll miss the turn, but you definitely won't miss the cliffs. Vermilion Cliffs National Monument stretches across northern Arizona and protects a landscape shaped over nearly 200 million years. The area became a national monument in 2000, helping safeguard fragile rock formations, prehistoric sites and habitats for rare wildlife. Coyote Buttes is the star attraction for many visitors. Its famous Wave is carved into Navajo Sandstone, which began as vast sand dunes during the Jurassic Period. Over millions of years, wind erosion, rainfall and temperature changes sculpted the flowing bands and curves seen today.

copyright: Traditional beach huts, Southwold, Suffolk Heritage Coast, England (© stevendocwra/Getty Images)
description: Along England's east shore, the Suffolk Heritage Coast blends windswept heaths, marshes, shingle beaches and expansive North Sea views. One of its best-known towns is Southwold, where water and history are inseparable. Almost encircled by the sea, the River Blyth and surrounding wetlands, the town occupies a slender peninsula shaped by centuries of fishing, trade and life at the edge of the water.

copyright: Horsehair parachute fungus, Belarus (© Máté/Nature Picture Library)
description: Fungi often go unnoticed beneath forest floors, lawns and fallen leaves, yet their underground threads help recycle nutrients and support healthy ecosystems. The mushrooms we see are only the fruiting bodies of much larger organisms. They appear briefly, release spores, then disappear from sight. Unlike plants, fungi belong to a kingdom of their own. Some species even glow, while others form partnerships with trees.

copyright: Sellin Pier, Rügen, Germany (© bluejayphoto/Getty Images)
description: When the first rays of sunlight gild the horizon, Sellin Pier reveals its most striking side. Located on the eastern coast of the island of Rügen in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, this structure is one of the best-known landmarks on Germany's Baltic coast. Its history dates back to 1906, when the first pier was opened. Over the decades, the structure suffered repeated damage from storms and other factors and was eventually demolished.

copyright: Whale shark and golden trevally, Cenderawasih Bay, West Papua, Indonesia (© Pete Oxford/Nature Picture Library)
description: Imagine coming face to face with a fish the size of a bus. The whale shark is the world's largest fish, yet it is a remarkably gentle giant. Despite its name, it is not a whale but a shark, with the biggest confirmed individuals measuring around 18 metres long and weighing more than 20 tonnes. Found in warm tropical and subtropical seas, whale sharks move slowly through the water with their mouths open, filtering plankton, fish eggs and other tiny prey. Their distinctive white spots and stripes form patterns unique to each individual, allowing researchers to identify and track them over time.
